description: interested in designing a website/software tool that helps visualize the changing weather conditions using the radar remote sensing data from NASA
summary: Radar Earth is an interactive website that turns NASA–ISRO NISAR radar data into simple, visual stories of how Earth's surface changes. Visitors spin a globe, switch layers for burn scars, floods and wetlands, and ground motion, and explore seven places on four continents with before/after radar sliders, image notes, a zoom lens and plain-language explanations of why each change happened and why it matters.
details:
What it does: Radar Earth shows three kinds of surface change using 2026 NISAR L-band data: wildfire burn scars (Utah, California, Spain), seasonal floods and wetlands (Bangladesh, Cambodia, Mali) and ground motion (Tokyo). Each place has a before/after comparison, measured numbers, and short explanations of the physical drivers and why the change matters to people.

NASA data used: NISAR Level-2 GCOV (radiometrically terrain-corrected backscatter) for fires and water, and Level-2 GUNW (geocoded unwrapped interferogram) for ground motion – all provisional L-band products downloaded from the Alaska Satellite Facility (ASF DAAC). Every scene name is listed on the website.

How I processed it: With Python (h5py, NumPy, Matplotlib, Pillow) I cropped the latitude/longitude browse images to each area using the scene footprint coordinates, and estimated open water by counting dark pixels (for example, Tonle Sap's open water grew from about 1% to 9% between June and October). For Tokyo, I converted the interferogram's phase to centimeters (phase × wavelength ÷ 4π), hid low-coherence pixels such as water, and removed the smooth trend caused by the ionosphere and atmosphere – showing that most of the raw signal over 12 days comes from the sky, not the ground.

What I learned: Burned forests lose their bright HV (cross-polarized) signal because the canopy that scattered the radar is gone; open water looks dark because it reflects radar away like a mirror; and interferograms need care because the atmosphere can look like ground motion.

Built with: HTML, CSS and JavaScript (no frameworks), hosted on GitHub Pages. Open source: https://github.com/Juneberrii/radar-earth

Limitations and next steps: Provisional data; water percentages are estimates from browse images. Next I would add time-series animations using NISAR's 12-day repeat, and stack many interferograms to measure millimeter-scale ground motion.
